mustard: Mustard gets its name from the Romans, who ground the seeds into grape must: mustum ardens, “burning must”. The popes at Avignon even kept an official mustard maker, the Grand Moutardier du Pape. One thing to know: heat kills its bite, so whisk it in off the flame when you finish a sauce.
duck: Here’s the trick with duck: score the fat, start it in a cold pan, and pour the fat off as it melts. Then roast your next potatoes in it. That’s the Southwest of France in one pan, the same place that keeps the bird in its own fat for confit.
mushroom: These started out underground in Paris. Under Napoleon, growers found that old quarry tunnels, cool, damp and dark, were perfect for mushrooms, and that’s where the French name comes from. When you cook them, don’t crowd the pan: packed together they steam, with room they brown.
rye: Rye started out as a weed in wheat and barley fields. As farming moved north into colder ground, the weed survived where the crop failed, so farmers just kept it. Soak the berries overnight before cooking, or they take well over an hour and stay hard in the middle.
chestnut: In mountain villages from Corsica to the Cévennes, they called it the “bread tree”: when wheat wouldn’t grow, chestnuts got ground into flour. Candy them and you get marron glacé, same nut, totally different life. Roasting them? Score a cross first or they explode.
goat-cheese: Goats were milked before cows, so this might be the oldest cheese family there is. In the Loire, the legend says the Saracens, stopped at Poitiers in 732, left their goats and their recipes behind. Young, it loves herbs and olive oil; aged, it wants honey and walnuts.
katsuobushi: This is bonito that’s simmered, smoked for weeks and dried with a mould until it’s the hardest food on Earth. A whole fillet literally rings like wood. Shave it into dashi with kombu and the umami you taste goes up nearly eightfold. Or put a handful on hot rice with soy sauce and watch the flakes dance in the steam.
strawberry: The strawberry you know was born in Brittany around 1750. A spy-engineer called Frézier smuggled a plant out of Chile, and it crossed with a Virginian one in French soil. Best part: his name sounds like fraisier, French for strawberry plant. Don’t wash them until the last minute.
silken-tofu: Kinugoshi means “silk-strained”, and neither word is true: no silk, no straining. The soy milk sets right in the box it’s sold in, so the name just describes how it feels. You can’t press it, so don’t try: drain it on a tilted plate for ten minutes instead.
apricot: Its Latin name blames Armenia, but the apricot comes from China, where people grew it four thousand years ago. Here’s what matters at the market: it doesn’t ripen after picking, it only softens. A hard, pale one will never get sweet, so buy by smell.
dill: Dill’s name goes back to Old Norse dilla, “to soothe”: people used it to calm colic. The North never let it go, and gravlax, salmon “buried” in salt and dill, is still its masterpiece. Dill hates heat and waiting, so snip it over the plate at the table, especially with yogurt, eggs or fish.
red-wine-vinegar: For most of history, vinegar was an accident rather than a product. Now you use it on purpose: deglaze a pan with it when you want the acidity to survive the reduction. As it cooks down, it keeps its edge.
saffron: Every crocus flower gives just three red threads, picked by hand at dawn before the sun wilts them. One gram takes about a hundred and fifty flowers, which is why it’s been worth more than gold for most of history. Steep the threads in warm water or stock for twenty minutes first; thrown in dry, half the perfume never wakes up.
fennel: The plain of Marathon is named after the Greek word for fennel, which grew wild there. So the famous run is basically named after a fennel field. Shave it raw and it crunches, fresh and a bit liquorice; braise it and it melts and goes gentle. Keep the fronds and use them like an herb.
rosemary: Rosemary means “dew of the sea”, after the coastal cliffs it clings to. Greek students wore rosemary crowns while studying, sure it helped their memory. In the kitchen it’s tough: tuck a sprig under roasting potatoes or lamb, and take it out before serving.
shrimp: Shrimp cook in about the time it takes to regret walking away: two minutes, until just pink and curled into a loose C. A tight O means you’ve gone too far. And keep the shells, that’s where the sweetness is: every head you throw away is a spoonful of bisque.
basil: Basil’s name comes from basileus, Greek for king. In India its cousin tulsi is sacred enough to grow in temple courtyards, and here it is on our tomatoes. Heat kills it, so tear the leaves by hand and add them off the flame, right at the end.
leek: Nero ate leeks in oil for days every month, sure they cleared his singing voice, and Romans called him the “leek-eater”. The white cooks down to silk, the green flavours your stock. Slit it lengthwise and rinse it well, because sand hides between the layers.
capers: A caper is a flower that never got to open. The buds are picked one by one at dawn from bushes growing out of stone walls, then cured in salt or brine. Salt-packed ones taste better, just rinse them well. Fry them crisp in olive oil and they turn into little savoury fireworks for fish.
peach: Its Latin name says “Persian”, but the peach is Chinese; the West just met it halfway along the trade routes. A ripe one smells ripe from a step away. Split it, grill it cut side down, and serve it with pretty much anything creamy.
fish-sauce: Fish sauce is just anchovies and salt, stacked in wooden barrels under the tropical sun for a year. Smell the bottle and you’ll worry, but trust the pot: once it cooks, the roar goes and pure depth stays. A teaspoon quietly makes a bolognese or a vinaigrette better.
pistachio: In Persia, lovers met under pistachio trees on moonlit nights, and hearing the shells crack open meant good luck. The greener the kernel, the better the pistachio; Sicily’s Bronte and Iran’s best are almost emerald. Crush them over anything creamy.
cider-vinegar: That cloudy strand floating in an unfiltered bottle is called the mother. It’s a living mat of bacteria and cellulose, not spoilage, and you can lift it out to start the next batch. Cider vinegar is gentle, so use a little more, with pork, cabbage or anything with apple in it.
negi: Japan is split over negi. In the east, growers pile soil up the stem for a long white shaft; in Kansai, kitchens want the green leaves. Try this: char the whole white part black over a flame, peel off the burnt layers, and the inside turns to jelly.
sage: Salvia comes from salvare, “to save”. The medieval school of Salerno asked: “Why should a man die who has sage in his garden?” In the kitchen it saves humbler things from blandness: pork, butter, beans. Fry whole leaves in butter until crisp: the butter goes nutty and the leaves turn into savoury chips.
wasabi: Most of what’s served as wasabi outside Japan is horseradish, mustard and green dye. The real thing is a rhizome grown in cold mountain streams, it takes two years, and it’s one of the hardest crops in the world to farm. Grated fresh, it loses its heat within fifteen minutes, which is why it’s grated right in front of you.
chickpeas: Cicero, Rome’s greatest speaker, got his family name from the chickpea, cicer. Supposedly an ancestor had a chickpea-shaped wart, and Cicero refused to change the name. Keep the cooking water: whip it and it foams like egg white.
turmeric: In India, turmeric dyes robes, brides get painted with it for luck, and it colours nearly every curry. Merchants happily sold it as “Indian saffron” for centuries. And watch your clothes: that stain is forever.
celery: The Greeks crowned athletes with celery leaves, and the Victorians served it in crystal vases as a luxury. Now it works quietly in every stock, one third of the French mirepoix. Don’t throw out the leaves: chop them like an herb over soups and salads.
nutmeg: Nutmeg once grew on ten tiny islands and nowhere else. In 1667 the Dutch gave Manhattan to the English to keep Run, a nutmeg island two miles long. Buy it whole, grate it straight over the dish, and stop sooner than you think: three passes season a whole béchamel.
peanut: The peanut isn’t a nut at all: it’s a legume that buries its own pods underground. Grind it with a little of its own oil and you’ve got the sauce behind half of West African and Southeast Asian cooking. Chilli and lime are its best friends.
rice-vinegar: Rice vinegar has around half the acidity of European vinegars. That’s why sushi rice can take a lot of it without going sharp. Check the label though: sushi vinegar already has sugar and salt in it, and using it as plain vinegar wrecks a dressing.
lard: Lard makes the flakiest pastry there is: its big fat crystals coat flour better than butter does. It ruled baking until vegetable shortening and marketing pushed it out. For pastry, ask for leaf lard, from around the kidneys; back fat is fine for frying but tastes of pork.
salmon: Salmon climbs waterfalls to die where it was born, and its Latin name may come from salire, “to leap”. Cook it less than you dare: the centre should still be silky. Keep it skin side down almost the whole way and the skin becomes the best part.
yuzu: Yuzu is gnarled, full of seeds, and gives barely a spoonful of juice, yet it perfumes a whole room. In Japan, people float whole yuzu in hot baths on the winter solstice. The zest is where the magic is: a few gratings over scallops or chocolate do what no lemon can.
tarragon: Tarragon’s name means “little dragon”: medieval healers said it cured snake bites, and its roots do coil like one. France built béarnaise sauce around its quiet anise flavour. Go easy, it takes over fast: a few leaves perfume a whole chicken.
grape: People domesticated the grape before writing, before the wheel, before most cities. Try frozen grapes on a summer day: each one is a tiny sorbet. Roasted, they go jammy and love cheese.
blue-cheese: One mould makes the whole blue family, from Roquefort to Stilton to Gorgonzola: Penicillium roqueforti. It’s needled into the wheel so air gets in, and the blue veins are its breathing paths. All that salt and power wants something sweet, like pears, figs or honey. Break some over a hot steak and you’ve got an instant sauce.
koikuchi-shoyu: Koikuchi is about four fifths of all the soy sauce Japan brews. It’s roughly half soybeans, half roasted wheat, and the wheat gives it that sweet, almost floral smell. Those aromas fade fast, so add it at the end, or in two goes. Once it’s open, keep it cold.
creme-fraiche: Crème fraîche is cream left to ripen with its own lactic bacteria until it thickens and turns a little sour. That acidity is the trick: it can boil in a sauce without splitting. It’s the safe cream for lemon or tomato, where ordinary cream will split.
miso: Samurai marched on miso: it travelled as dry rations and turned into instant soup. Every region had its own, white and sweet in Kyoto, dark and fierce in the north. Never boil it, heat kills its aromas, so whisk it in at the end.
shiso: That jagged leaf next to your sashimi isn’t decoration, it’s a palate cleanser. It’s mint’s Japanese cousin, and it tastes like cumin, basil and citrus all at once. Roll a few leaves and slice them thin at the last second, then scatter them over rice, tuna or strawberries.
cardamom: Vikings found cardamom in the markets of Constantinople and carried it north. That’s why, a thousand years later, Scandinavia bakes with more of it per person than anywhere outside Asia. Crush the green pods to get at the black seeds, and grind only those.
mango: India has grown mangoes for four thousand years, and its leaders still send crates of the best ones to neighbouring heads of state. People call it “mango diplomacy”. Try ripe mango with chilli, salt and lime, then try green mango shredded: it’s practically a different ingredient.
clove: In Han dynasty China, courtiers held cloves in their mouths before speaking to the emperor, so their breath would be worthy. Here’s the old French trick: stud an onion with two or three cloves and drop it into a broth or béchamel. You get depth without seeing any spice.
flour-t65: T65 is the flour of the baguette de tradition française. A 1993 decree says that baguette holds flour, water, salt and yeast, and nothing else. The extra bran feeds the fermentation, so the dough rises faster and tastes of more. Hold back a little water at first: it takes up less than it looks.
oregano: Oregano is Greek for “joy of the mountain”, and it grew on hillsides long before pizza. When American soldiers came home from Italy in 1945, they asked for “the pizza herb”, and sales went up five thousand percent in a decade. It’s one of the few herbs that’s stronger dried. Warm it in oil first to wake up the perfume.
beetroot: The Romans only ate the leaves and left the root to medicine. Then British blockades cut Napoleon off from cane sugar, he had thousands of hectares of beet planted, and the root became Europe’s sugar bowl. Roast it whole in its skin; once it’s cooked, the skin rubs off with your thumb.
foie-gras: The word for liver in French, Italian and Spanish comes from this dish. Rome fed geese figs and called it iecur ficatum, “fig liver”, and ficatum became foie, fegato, hígado. Sear slices in a dry, very hot pan for a minute a side: the fat it lets out is a sauce on its own.
white-beans: Tuscans love beans so much the rest of Italy nicknamed them mangiafagioli, the bean-eaters. Cook them gently, because a hard boil bursts their skins, with a bay leaf and a whole garlic clove. And keep the broth: it’s liquid silver.
prosciutto: Cato the Elder wrote down the method twenty-two centuries ago: salt, air, time. Nothing has been added since. Around Parma, the hams hang in tall shuttered houses so the breeze off the Apennines can finish what the salt started. Slice it thin enough to read through and serve it at room temperature, with figs, melon or peaches.
fleur-de-sel-guerande: Fleur de sel forms as a thin crust on top of the salt pan on dry days, and the salt worker, the paludier, lifts it off with a flat wooden board without touching the clay floor. Never cook with it and never put it in a liquid: the crunch is the whole point. Add it once the plate is off the heat, and keep it in a closed pot.
ricotta: Ricotta isn’t strictly a cheese: it’s made from the whey left after cheesemaking, heated again until the last proteins come up. The name says it: ricotta, recooked. Drain it in a sieve for an hour before it goes into a filling, or the water comes out in the oven and ruins the pastry.
cornichon: French cornichons are picked at three or four centimetres and pickled in vinegar with tarragon and pearl onions, which makes them sharp. An American dill pickle is brined and sour instead, and you can’t swap one for the other. Chop them into a gribiche or rémoulade at the last moment, or they leak vinegar and thin the sauce.
cabbage: Cato the Elder filled pages of his farming manual with cabbage, sure it could cure all kinds of things. Its real gift came later: salted and packed, it got northern Europe and the Royal Navy through winters without scurvy. Cook it fast and hot or long and slow, never in between, because the middle is where the sulphur smell lives.
balsamic: In Modena’s attics, cooked grape must rests for decades in a row of shrinking barrels: oak, chestnut, cherry. Families started a set of barrels when a daughter was born, her dowry, aged twenty-five years. The real thing is syrup-thick, so just a few drops on strawberries or parmesan.
corn: Nine thousand years ago, Mexican farmers started turning teosinte, a grass with a dozen hard seeds, into cobs with hundreds. They planted it with beans and squash, the “three sisters”. Fresh corn starts losing its sweetness the hour it’s picked, so cook it the day you buy it.
butternut: The butternut has a birth certificate: Charles Leggett bred it in Stow, Massachusetts, in 1944. He said it was smooth as butter and sweet as a nut, and named it on the spot. The neck is solid flesh and the base is all seeds, so cut them apart and treat them as two different vegetables.
porcini: Porcini means “little pigs” in Italian, for those plump stems. Nobody farms them: every one on a plate was found by someone walking through a forest, and good spots are secrets people take to the grave. Dried, they’re a pantry treasure, and the soaking water is a broth on its own, so never pour it away.
clementine: The clementine turned up around 1900 in an orphanage garden near Oran, found by Brother Clément Rodier while he tended the trees. It was a chance seedling, seedless and sweeter than its neighbours, and it carries his name. Buy them with the leaves still on: it’s the only reliable sign of freshness on citrus at the market.
walnut: Because a walnut looks like a brain, medieval doctors prescribed it for head problems. The theory was nonsense, but the walnut fed them anyway. Buy them in the shell, since shelled ones go rancid fast, and give them ten seconds in a hot pan: they taste twice as much of themselves.
persimmon: Some persimmons are inedible until they’re almost liquid: the tannins that dry your mouth only break down when most people would throw the fruit out. So learn which one you’ve got. Fuyu is squat and eaten firm, like an apple; Hachiya is pointed and has to be spoon-soft.
brussels-sprout: The Brussels sprout people remember hating doesn’t exist anymore. In the 1990s, Dutch breeders found the compounds behind the bitterness and bred them down. Halve them and roast them cut side down until properly brown: boiling is what gave them their reputation.
